source.title: Pre-training under infinite compute
source.authors: Konwoo Kim; Suhas Kotha; Percy Liang; Tatsunori Hashimoto

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling of held-out loss under data constraints and refines the power-law claim: standard epoching and parameter scaling can overfit, while carefully tuned regularization produces a monotone parameter-scaling fit. It also reports downstream evaluations, but does not test compute-optimal parameter-token allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports numerous scaling-curve points only in figures; where the text gives no numeric point, rows below record the figure-only evidence and the authors' stated trend. It also cites prior scaling-law results, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to held-out loss in a fixed-data, repeated-epoch regime. It shows the standard recipe overfits, contrary to the Muennighoff epoch-decay form. It shows the parameter-scaling law, and its exponent (1.02 vs Chinchilla's 0.34), depend on jointly tuning regularization at each size. It fits data-scaling laws on recipe asymptotes and checks that downstream accuracy tracks validation loss. These results bear on V1 (data axis), V5 (repeated data), V6 and V7. Compute-optimal allocation (V3), architecture shape (V4) and large-scale validation of extrapolation (V2) are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. It should add the headline estimates: the joint recipe's asymptote is 5.17× more data-efficient than the standard recipe, and data-scaling laws with similar exponents suggest the gain persists at larger token counts. Distilling an ensemble into a 300M student keeps 83% of the ensemble gain. The 4B-token CPT ensemble beats 73B-token default CPT (17.5× data efficiency). The authors propose judging recipes by scaling-law asymptotes rather than by compute-budget performance.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than testing compute-optimal allocation as in the original scaling-law studies, this paper fixes seed-data budgets, tunes regularization and epochs, and fits loss curves to estimate infinite-parameter or infinite-ensemble asymptotes. It also evaluates ensembling, distillation, and continued pre-training.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss trends depend on regularization and hyperparameter tuning at each model size. Ensemble asymptotes depend on member epoch count and weight decay; the preferred settings differ from the single-model optimum. Architecture is not controlled across sizes, and the authors note that the 1.4B model trades depth for width.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss of a logit-averaged ensemble falls as roughly 1/K in member count, reaching an asymptote of 3.34 (3.27 when tuned), below the parameter-scaling asymptote of 3.43.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss scales as a power law in ensemble member count, with a lower asymptote than parameter scaling under fixed data.

record.problems: The authors describe data-scaling laws as noisy and the multi-tier asymptote estimates as rough. Their sensitivity analysis does not test the two-tier and three-tier joint-scaling fits. The parameter sweep spans 150M–1.4B, and the paper does not validate asymptote predictions against much larger runs. The 1.4B architecture has a non-standard depth/width tradeoff.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted individual figure-only points for the various parameter counts, ensemble sizes, and token budgets; the paper's text does not state their exact values. Also omitted the separate per-benchmark scores for the downstream table and most intermediate K values for the CPT table; summary averages and the key reported comparisons are retained. Relevant figures and tables: Figures 2–8, 10–11; Tables 1 and 5.

untested.parts: Parameter and compute axes with data not the bottleneck; the several-orders-of-magnitude range (data axis spans only 200M–1.6B).
Whole version. Asymptotes are extrapolated but never checked against much larger runs.
Whole version; compute-optimal allocation is not studied.
Whole version. The 1.4B model's depth/width differs, but this is not a controlled comparison.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer; the power-law form in the CPT setting.
A fitted quantitative loss-to-downstream predictor, and predictability for CPT math benchmarks.

missing.what: Downstream averages across model sizes: the unregularized series (54.35/55.34/53.42/54.14) is non-monotone like its loss, while the regularized series (55.12/58.39/59.95/60.73) is monotone.
Parameter-scaling power laws fitted at all four token counts share exponents close to 1.
Seed sensitivity of the parameter-scaling asymptote (at most 0.02 across 3 seeds); the two- and three-tier fits are not tested and the authors call them rough.
The standard recipe's best loss at each token count comes from 600M, with 1.4B within about 0.02 loss; the data-scaling points for the standard recipe.

record.verdict_notes: The key correction is that the fixed 200M-token setting makes data the bottleneck, so R1–R3 do not test V1. Kaplan's Fig. 9 already predicts a plateau there. They are re-linked to V5 (repeated data) and V7. V1 is tested only on the data axis (R7), using noisy asymptote-of-asymptote fits over about one order of magnitude. The CPT rows are comparisons of the study's own interventions, so they are unlinked. The 1.4B model uses a non-standard depth/width, which the authors acknowledge.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter scaling with fixed seed-token budgets and data scaling of recipe asymptotes; does not test loss scaling with training compute or establish a power law across several orders of magnitude.
The paper extrapolates fitted curves to asymptotes but does not validate those predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitted runs.
Does not optimize parameter and token allocation at fixed compute budgets or measure their growth with compute.
Does not conduct a controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies repeated-data pre-training and continued pre-training, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds across those regimes or in other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests downstream benchmark performance for selected pre-trained models and continued-pre-training runs; does not fit or validate a quantitative predictor mapping pre-training loss to downstream performance.
Tests sensitivity to regularization and hyperparameter tuning, and observes overfitting in some settings; does not systematically compare published exponents or fitting methods across studies.

rows.subject: 300M model
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the fixed seed corpus for increasing epoch counts under the standard recipe.
rows.value: Loss initially decreases, but starts increasing at sufficiently high epoch counts.
rows.note: The text explicitly attributes the later increase to overfitting; individual plotted loss values are not stated.
rows.check: Data is the bottleneck here (200M tokens), so this is not V1's condition. It bears on V5 (repeated data): loss rises at high epoch counts, contrary to the monotone decay-based law of Muennighoff et al., which the authors say it disagrees with.

source_check.correct: V5: reversed at sufficiently high epoch counts. V7: observed fit-dependence; the epoch curve contradicts the monotone decay-based functional form.
source_check.problem: The reversed state fits V5, but not the simultaneously linked V7.

rows.subject: 150M, 300M, 600M, and 1.4B models
rows.operation_detail: Increased parameter count while tuning learning rate and epoch count at each size under the standard recipe.
rows.value: Increasing parameter count did not significantly decrease loss; the 1.4B model performed worse than the 600M model, and a 10× increase in parameter count improved loss by less than 0.1.
rows.note: The authors report this result despite tuning epoch count and learning rate separately for each parameter count.
rows.check: Data is the bottleneck, so this does not test V1; Kaplan's own Fig. 9 predicts this plateau, as the authors note. For repeated-data parameter scaling under weight decay 0.1, a 10× parameter increase gains <0.1 loss and 1.4B is worse than 600M, so no clean power law appears. State changed from reversed to absent, since the change is mostly flat with one reversal.

source_check.correct: V5: absent overall, with the 1.4B model worse than 600M. V7: observed dependence on regularization and tuning.
source_check.problem: The absent state fits the repeated-data scaling effect, but V7's setup dependence is observed.

rows.subject: 150M, 300M, 600M, and 1.4B models
rows.operation_detail: Jointly tuned weight decay, learning rate, and epoch count at each parameter count, then fit validation loss as a power law in parameter count.
rows.measure: Held-out validation loss as a function of parameter count
rows.baseline: The standard recipe; its fitted asymptote is 3.75.
rows.value: The regularized recipe's fitted asymptote is 3.43; the text reports a parameter-scaling exponent of 1.02.
rows.uncertainty: Asymptote estimates varied by at most 0.02 loss across 3 seeds.
rows.note: The fitted trend is monotone over the tested sizes, but the tested parameter range is not several orders of magnitude.
rows.check: Data is the bottleneck (fitted asymptote 3.43), so this bears on V5 (repeated-data regime) and V7 (exponent 1.02 vs Chinchilla's 0.34), not V1. Within the tested range 150M–1.4B the power law holds, so observed. The narrow range is an untested part, not a partial result. The 3.75 baseline belongs to the standard recipe, which is not monotone.

source_check.correct: Standard recipe best-loss estimate: 3.75, selected by tuning learning rate, epochs and parameter count; not a fitted parameter-scaling asymptote. Regularized fitted asymptote: 3.43; parameter exponent: 1.02; cited Chinchilla exponent: 0.34; asymptote variation across three seeds: at most 0.02.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3; Section 4.3; Section 5.1; Appendix D.1 and Figure 18.
source_check.problem: The baseline number is correct, but describing 3.75 as a fitted asymptote is incorrect.

rows.subject: 300M ensemble members
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of independently trained ensemble members and fit loss as a power law in member count.

conditions.value: K increased; individual plotted values not stated

rows.measure: Held-out validation loss as a function of ensemble member count
rows.value: The ensemble loss decreases close to a rate of 1/K; its K→∞ asymptote is 3.34.
rows.note: The asymptote is based on a fitted curve, not a directly trained infinite-member ensemble.
rows.check: Scaling the number of ensemble members is not parameter, token or compute scaling of a single LM. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: 300M ensemble members
rows.operation_detail: Compared ensemble scaling curves after varying member epoch count and weight decay, and selected hyperparameters for the K→∞ asymptote.

conditions.value: More epochs and less weight decay than the single-model optimum

rows.measure: Held-out validation loss and fitted K→∞ asymptote
rows.value: Selecting hyperparameters for the ensemble asymptote improves it to 3.27.
rows.note: The ranking of hyperparameter choices changes with ensemble member count.
rows.check: Tuning ensemble hyperparameters is the study's own method compared against alternatives; it bears on no version.

rows.subject: Joint parameter- and ensemble-scaling recipe
rows.size_stated: Parameter count and ensemble member count both taken to infinity
rows.operation_detail: Fit power laws over ensemble member count, then fit a second power law over parameter count using the first fit's asymptotes.
rows.baseline: Regularized recipe asymptote: 3.43; unregularized recipe asymptote: 3.75.
rows.uncertainty: The authors advise treating the multi-tier asymptote estimates as rough estimates.
rows.note: This is an extrapolated asymptote. The study does not check the prediction against runs at much larger parameter counts or member counts.
rows.check: This is an extrapolated two-tier ensemble asymptote that is never validated against larger runs, so it does not test V2. It is the study's own method's estimate.

rows.subject: Standard, regularized, and joint-scaling recipes
rows.operation_detail: Fit data-scaling power laws to recipe-level estimates of best possible loss across seed-token budgets.

conditions.value: Standard best-run losses or regularized/joint-scaling asymptotes

rows.measure: Held-out validation loss as a function of seed-token count
rows.value: The three data-scaling laws have exponents between 0.23 and 0.24 and asymptotes between 1.89 and 1.96.
rows.uncertainty: The authors describe the data-scaling laws as noisy.
rows.note: The text gives ranges across the three recipes rather than assigning each exponent and asymptote to a particular recipe.
rows.check: Loss falls as a power law in seed tokens, with parameters and compute taken to the non-bottleneck limit. Exponents are 0.23–0.24, but the range is 200M–1.6B (about one order of magnitude) and the fits are built on asymptote estimates that the authors call noisy. The values are given as ranges across recipes.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 5.1–5.4, Figures 7–8: seed budgets 200M, 400M, 800M and 1.6B; exponents 0.23–0.24; asymptotes 1.89–1.96.

rows.subject: Models at four parameter counts
rows.operation_detail: Compared parameter-scaling fits using default weight decay, weight decay tuned only at 150M, epoch count tuned only at 150M, or all relevant hyperparameters tuned at each scale.

conditions.value: Hyperparameter transfer across model sizes versus tuning separately at each size

rows.measure: Held-out validation loss across parameter counts
rows.baseline: Joint tuning of learning rate, epoch count, and weight decay at each parameter count.
rows.value: Fixing weight decay at 0.1 fails to give clean scaling; transferring the 150M optimal weight decay produces non-monotone scaling; transferring the 150M optimal epoch count plateaus sooner.
rows.note: The paper says joint tuning at each scale is necessary for clean scaling.
rows.check: This shows clearly that whether clean scaling appears depends on the tuning procedure: with transferred hyperparameters it is non-monotone or plateaus. For V7 this is observed, not partial.

source_check.correct: V7: observed. For V5, separate conditions: default weight decay gives no significant parameter-scaling improvement; transferred weight decay gives non-monotone scaling; transferred epoch count gives earlier saturation.
source_check.problem: Observed describes V7's tuning dependence, but does not describe V5's scaling effect across these failure and saturation conditions.

rows.subject: Pre-trained models, ensembles, and distilled models
rows.size_stated: 150M, 300M, 600M, and 1.4B models; ensemble sizes also varied
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated held-out validation loss and downstream benchmark error on the same models.
rows.measure: Relationship between validation loss and average downstream benchmark error
rows.value: The authors state that models with lower validation loss have lower average error; regularized-model downstream accuracy scales smoothly, and increasing ensemble parameter or member count improves performance.
rows.note: The figure description reports the trend but does not provide numerical validation-loss values for individual points.
rows.check: Figure-only evidence. The authors state that lower validation loss goes with lower downstream error.

rows.subject: Unregularized 300M model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated accuracy on three downstream benchmarks and reported the average.
rows.note: The table reports the benchmark average and individual benchmark scores.
rows.check: Comparator only. On its own it shows nothing about predictability. The unregularized series (54.35, 55.34, 53.42, 54.14) is non-monotone in N, tracking the loss; that series is not recorded.

rows.subject: Regularized 1.4B model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated accuracy on three downstream benchmarks and reported the average.
rows.note: The table identifies this as the 1.4B entry under Model scaling.

rows.subject: 1.4B, K=5 ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated ensemble accuracy on three downstream benchmarks and reported the average.
rows.note: This is the highest average accuracy among the listed pre-training model and ensemble entries.
rows.check: The ensemble is the study's method, but lower loss going with higher accuracy bears on V6 as loss-predictability.

rows.subject: 300M student distilled from an ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated student accuracy on three downstream benchmarks and reported the average.
rows.note: The paper reports this as the Ensemble distillation entry.
rows.check: Distilled model; it bears on V6 only through the loss–accuracy correspondence.

rows.note: The table labels this reference column Llama 3B.
rows.check: Base-model reference for the CPT intervention comparisons; no scale or loss relationship.
